newsitem.title: USA: White House suggests Britain give IRA signal.
newsitem.headline: White House suggests Britain give IRA signal.

text.p: The White House suggested on Monday Britain should send a signal to encourage the Irish Republican Army to restore its ceasefire, as President Bill Clinton condemned the latest killing in Northern Ireland.
Clinton, recovering from a torn tendon, issued a statement denouncing the "horrific" murder of a Catholic in Belfast last week as Vice President Al Gore met with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton.

Gore was asked by a reporter whether he supported Sen. Edward Kennedy's call last week for Britain to declare that if the IRA restored its ceasefire its political wing, Sinn Fein, would be admitted to the Northern Ireland peace talks.

"Well, that's a decision for the British government to make," Gore said. "These are all delicate matters and there are ways to signal that thought without encountering the kinds of problems which they (Britain) evidently fear might make them reluctant to spell it out explicitly."

"But let me say on behalf of President Bill Clinton and the United States of America that we have the absolute conviction and certainty that should the IRA declare a ceasefire, then Sinn Fein would be invited to participate in the talks. Now, how that expression comes from others is for them to decide," the vice president said.

Sinn Fein is currently excluded from the talks, scheduled to resume on June 3, because of the IRA's refusal to renew a ceasefire in its armed campaign to rid Northern Ireland of British rule. The IRA abandoned a 17-month truce a year ago.
Michael Ancram, Britain's minister of state for Northern Ireland appeared cool however to the Kennedy approach when he spoke to journalists at the British Embassy on Monday morning.

Ancram, in Washington for regular contacts with the administration and Congress and to attend St Patrick's Day celebrations, said Britain could issue an invitation to Sinn Fein to come to the talks only after the IRA met the conditions that applied to all parties, principally a firm commitment to non-violence.

Ancram said even if the IRA declared a ceasefire, given the reversal of their earlier ceasefire, it was essential for it to be demonstrated they were undertaking "no actions that are inconsistent with a ceasefire." He said that while the last ceasefire was in place the IRA was testing new mortars in the Republic of Ireland.
Ancram said the series of attacks by IRA guerrillas in recent months left him little hope that a ceasefire might be declared soon.

Bruton was to have seen Clinton on Monday but the president has cut back his schedule while recovering from surgery for a torn tendon. Administration officials said Clinton still might see Bruton later on Monday at a White House St. Patrick's Day party.
Clinton's statement condemning the murder of John Shane, a Roman Catholic father of nine, said he hoped British authorities would find who was responsible.
"This horrific killing deserves universal condemnation," Clinton said. "I hope the British authorities will quickly identify who is responsible.
"Nothing worth having in Northern Ireland can be achieved by killing and maiming, terror and threats," Clinton added.

"I urge the people of both communities to make known in every way they can their repudiation of violence by any group, for any reason. I will continue to stand with those who stand for peace, today as we commemorate the saint who brought the message of peace to Ireland, and every day."
Sinn Fein blamed Loyalist guerrillas for the murder and said it was evidence that a shaky 29-month Loyalist ceasefire had ended, but allies of pro-British units denied it.

In response to a journalist's question, Bruton said he found "very significant" new reports that British soldiers were given "shoot to kill" orders on the eve of "Bloody Sunday" in 1972, when 13 unarmed Northern Ireland demonstrators were killed by army gunfire.
"This evidence, if verified, is very significant," Bruton said. "It suggests that there was a very high degree of deliberation involved in the killings that occurred."
He said he was anxious to go through the matter "in the form of due process, assembling all the evidence," but the new information justified a "radical reassessment" of events.
